payload.throughline: Map the argument, test conclusion fit, weigh passage evidence, bound generalizations, and require a passage-grounded causal link.

curriculum_context.canonical_title: Evaluate Passage Logic, Evidence, Generalization, and Causality

learner_content_blocks: Starting check: locate the conclusion. This low-stakes check does not select a route, satisfy an exit, or establish mastery.
Goal: test an argument from the inside—what follows from the passage’s own claims—without replacing the author’s premises with outside knowledge.
Prerequisite check: first distinguish the conclusion from its support and map the stated relation. If that mapping is not secure, stop and return to V3-LES-386478 under V3-EDG-192746.
Reconstruct the argument as premises → bridge → conclusion. Then ask whether accepting the premises makes the conclusion reasonable, merely possible, or unsupported.
Plausibility asks whether a claim could fit the passage. Soundness within this bounded task asks whether the stated support and bridge actually warrant the conclusion.
Respect qualifiers. “Often,” “in these cases,” and “unless” limit what follows. Do not strengthen a qualified premise into an absolute conclusion.
Mental model: conclusion fit is a load test. Put only passage-supplied support on one side and the exact conclusion on the other; any missing bridge or enlarged claim is visible.

Think aloud: the passage says a plan reduced delays in two offices, then concludes the plan can reduce delays where the same bottleneck exists. That is qualified. I reject the stronger reading that it will eliminate every delay everywhere.

Worked example: “All archived letters in this collection are catalogued. Document M is an archived letter in this collection. Therefore Document M is catalogued.” If the premises are accepted, the conclusion follows directly.

Selection reasoning: the conclusion neither adds a new criterion nor widens the set. An alternative conclusion about the document’s historical value would require a premise the passage never supplied.
Guided practice: use the visible passage-boundary checklist, then commit before feedback.
Less help: apply the same evaluation with one brief non-answer-bearing cue.
On your own: evaluate a fresh passage argument without answer-bearing assistance.
Boundary: an argument can be internally well supported even if the reader doubts a premise outside the passage. Conversely, a familiar or agreeable conclusion can still be unsupported by the text.
Near exit: evaluate a closely aligned fresh passage using the taught model.
Changed exit: preserve the same evaluative construct while the passage relation or required operation changes.
Near-function repair: Compare the exact demand of the conclusion with the conditions, scope, and certainty actually supplied. The cue does not disclose the fresh re-entry.
Fresh near-function re-entry: evaluate an unexposed passage with no answer-bearing help.
Changed-function repair: Use the counterexample to remove the absolute claim; do not manufacture a new absolute conclusion. The cue does not disclose the fresh re-entry.
Fresh changed-function re-entry: recheck the exact failed function in a new passage.
Bounded stop: after one fresh re-entry miss, do not loop or award exit credit. Return control to the planner for later support.
Recap: identify the exact conclusion, preserve every qualifier, locate the bridge from support to conclusion, and judge only the fit licensed by the passage.

Prerequisite handoff: the argument elements or their relations were not mapped securely. Stop this lesson and return to V3-LES-386478; do not substitute an in-lesson summary for the canonical prerequisite.
Starting check: identify relevant evidence. This low-stakes check does not select a route, satisfy an exit, or establish mastery.
Goal: ask three separate questions—what evidence is present, whether it bears on the claim, and whether it is enough for the claim’s exact strength.
Bridge from V3-LES-386478: first map the claim and supporting passage part; if that mapping is unavailable, use the existing prerequisite handoff rather than guessing.
Presence is not relevance: a detail can be true in the passage yet fail to change confidence in the target claim.
Relevance is not sufficiency: evidence may bear directly on a claim but remain too narrow for an absolute or broad conclusion.
Absence supports a claim only when the passage gives a reason the missing feature should have appeared and describes a search or observation capable of finding it.
Mental model: claim target → predicted evidence → observed passage detail → strength match. Mark each link separately.

Think aloud: attendance rose after the schedule change, so the evidence is relevant to access. But the passage also reports a simultaneous fare reduction, so attendance alone is not sufficient to isolate the schedule as the only explanation.

Worked example: claim—“The guide’s warning changed the travelers’ route.” Evidence—the travelers quote the warning, discuss its risk, and immediately choose the alternate road. Those details are relevant and jointly support the bounded claim.
Selection reasoning: a description of the road’s color would be present evidence but irrelevant to whether the warning changed the choice.
Guided practice: use the visible passage-boundary checklist, then commit before feedback.
Less help: apply the same evaluation with one brief non-answer-bearing cue.
On your own: evaluate a fresh passage argument without answer-bearing assistance.
Boundary: missing mention is not automatically evidence of absence. The passage must establish that the author looked where the feature should have appeared or that the account aimed to be complete.
Near exit: evaluate a closely aligned fresh passage using the taught model.
Changed exit: preserve the same evaluative construct while the passage relation or required operation changes.
Near-function repair: First test whether the detail changes confidence in the claim; then test whether the full set warrants the claim’s strength. The cue does not disclose the fresh re-entry.
Fresh near-function re-entry: evaluate an unexposed passage with no answer-bearing help.
Changed-function repair: When the claim names a reason, evidence must connect that reason to the outcome rather than merely repeat the outcome. The cue does not disclose the fresh re-entry.
Fresh changed-function re-entry: recheck the exact failed function in a new passage.
Bounded stop: after one fresh re-entry miss, do not loop or award exit credit. Return control to the planner for later support.
Recap: inventory what is present, connect it to the exact claim, compare evidence strength with claim strength, and treat silence cautiously.
Starting check: preserve the observed group. This low-stakes check does not select a route, satisfy an exit, or establish mastery.
Goal: draw a scope box around the evidence, then ask whether the generalization stays inside that box.
Bridge from argument mapping: identify the basis and conclusion first; unresolved mapping returns to V3-LES-386478 through the lesson’s prerequisite handoff.
Track four scope dimensions: who or what was observed, where, when, and under which stated conditions.
Quantifiers matter. “Some,” “most in this set,” and “all” are different claims. A conclusion may cautiously extend to similar cases only when the passage supplies the similarity condition.
Do not import outside counterexamples. The defect is visible when the claim outruns the passage basis.
Mental model: evidence scope box versus claim scope box. A warranted generalization fits within or explicitly qualifies any extension beyond the evidence box.

Think aloud: the passage reports one winter program in four rural schools. A conclusion about those schools during that winter fits; a claim about all schools in every season expands population, setting, and time at once.

Worked example: six neighborhood markets in one district extended hours and reported later customer visits. “These markets received later visits after extending hours” stays within the basis. “Every retailer should expect the same result” does not.
Selection reasoning: the warranted statement preserves the observed set and timing rather than changing a local pattern into a universal forecast.
Guided practice: use the visible passage-boundary checklist, then commit before feedback.
Less help: apply the same evaluation with one brief non-answer-bearing cue.
On your own: evaluate a fresh passage argument without answer-bearing assistance.
Boundary: a narrow conclusion is not automatically weak; it can be exactly as broad as the evidence warrants. Mentioning a larger group does not warrant a claim about that whole group.
Near exit: evaluate a closely aligned fresh passage using the taught model.
Changed exit: preserve the same evaluative construct while the passage relation or required operation changes.
Near-function repair: Use a five-part scope box so any unsupported expansion has a named dimension. The cue does not disclose the fresh re-entry.
Fresh near-function re-entry: evaluate an unexposed passage with no answer-bearing help.
Changed-function repair: Carry the quantifier and population together; “some selected members” cannot become “all” or “most everywhere.” The cue does not disclose the fresh re-entry.
Fresh changed-function re-entry: recheck the exact failed function in a new passage.
Bounded stop: after one fresh re-entry miss, do not loop or award exit credit. Return control to the planner for later support.
Recap: mark population, setting, time, conditions, and quantifier in both evidence and conclusion; reject or revise every unsupported expansion.
Starting check: identify causal language. This low-stakes check does not select a route, satisfy an exit, or establish mastery.
Goal: identify exactly what the passage claims caused what, then inspect whether the passage supplies a link stronger than sequence or co-occurrence alone.
Bridge from V3-LES-386478: map the two events and their asserted relation before evaluation; failure uses the exact V3-LES-386478 handoff.
A causal claim says changing one factor produced a change in another. “After,” “alongside,” and “was associated with” do not by themselves say caused.

Within a passage, a causal link becomes more warranted when the text supplies direct intervention, removal-and-return, a traced mechanism, or an explicit contrast while addressing passage-mentioned alternatives.
Do not demand outside methods coursework. Judge the relation and evidence the passage actually supplies.
Mental model: proposed cause → linkage evidence → outcome, with passage-supplied alternatives placed beside the link rather than ignored.

Think aloud: waits fell after a policy change, but the passage says staffing increased the same day. Sequence makes the policy relevant, yet the staffing change is a passage-supplied alternative, so the policy-alone causal claim is not warranted.

Worked example: a door begins sticking only when a new seal is installed, moves freely when the seal is removed, and sticks again when the seal is replaced. The repeated change with installation status directly supports the bounded claim that this seal causes the sticking.
Selection reasoning: mere timing would be weaker; the removal-and-return pattern supplies the causal link.
Guided practice: use the visible passage-boundary checklist, then commit before feedback.
Less help: apply the same evaluation with one brief non-answer-bearing cue.
On your own: evaluate a fresh passage argument without answer-bearing assistance.
Boundary: causation need not be absolute or universal. A passage may warrant that one factor contributed under stated conditions while leaving other factors possible.
Near exit: evaluate a closely aligned fresh passage using the taught model.
Changed exit: preserve the same evaluative construct while the passage relation or required operation changes.

Near-function repair: Sequence establishes order; causal linkage requires evidence that the proposed factor produced the outcome under the passage conditions. The cue does not disclose the fresh re-entry.
Fresh near-function re-entry: evaluate an unexposed passage with no answer-bearing help.
Changed-function repair: A removal-and-return pattern tests whether the outcome follows the proposed factor across changes. The cue does not disclose the fresh re-entry.
Fresh changed-function re-entry: recheck the exact failed function in a new passage.
Bounded stop: after one fresh re-entry miss, do not loop or award exit credit. Return control to the planner for later support.
Recap: name cause and outcome, separate sequence from linkage, inspect passage-supplied alternatives, and match causal strength to the evidence.
